entry.title: Sūcī: A Bibliography Manager with Indic Characteristics

link.title: Sūcī: A Bibliography Manager with Indic Characteristics

entry.content:
This post is the last of a series on the items in the Assets menu of this website, which I have written over the last two months together with Claude.

What it is

Sūcī is a program for managing a bibliography. The name is the Sanskrit word सूची, which means “list” or “index,” and also “needle.”

It works with bibliography files in the BibTeX and BibLaTeX formats. These were created for use with LaTeX, but the format is simple plain text and has become a general standard that many online services and other bibliography programs can read and write, so Sūcī may be useful even to people who do not use LaTeX. It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows.

Background

The Suśruta Project’s publications, and the citations on this website, are generated from a BibLaTeX file of about 6,700 entries (it can be searched online, as described in an earlier post). For many years I have maintained it with JabRef, a capable program to which I owe a great deal. I unhesitatingly recommend JabRef to anyone working on a bibliography, and it many situations it will be a better choice than Sūcī. But general-purpose bibliography managers are not designed with Indology in mind. They do not know that śāstra should be found when one types “sastra,” or that ā follows a and not z, or that a title such as Nyāya-vaiśeṣika should not be “corrected” when titles are capitalised. They look up books in catalogues that are weak on Indian publications. And much of our older literature is now read as scans at the Internet Archive, which need to be cited by a stable identifier.

Sūcī was started in October 2026 to deal with these things.

What it does

  • Speed. The 6,700-entry library opens in about a quarter of a second.
  • Care with the file. Entries that have not been edited are saved exactly as they were, byte for byte. Sūcī reads and writes the same files as JabRef, so one can move between the two freely. A backup is kept at every save.
  • Searching without diacritics. “sastra” finds śāstra. One can also search for phrases, particular fields and ranges of years.
  • Sanskrit alphabetical order is available as a sort order: a ā i ī u ū ṛ … k kh g gh ṅ … ś ṣ s h.
  • Adding an entry from a DOI or ISBN. ISBNs are looked up in the K10plus/GVK union catalogue, Open Library and Google Books together, and one chooses the best record.
  • Finding a DOI or ISBN from a title. Open-access copies are offered first, and book reviews are not mistaken for the book.
  • Internet Archive scans. The ARK identifier of a scan is stored in the entry and opens in the browser with one click. Multi-volume works can have a separate identifier for each volume.
  • Formatted citations in Chicago, New Hart’s Rules and other styles, with italics, ready to paste into an email or a word-processor document.
  • Capitalisation of English titles that leaves Sanskrit terms, and titles in other languages and scripts, alone.
  • Conversion of LaTeX accents to Unicode and back.
  • An integrity check that finds missing fields, duplicate keys, bad ISBNs and similar problems, and can repair many of them.

Sūcī does not have JabRef’s groups or full-text search of PDFs, and it does not connect directly to Word or LibreOffice.

Getting it

There are installers for Linux and Windows on the releases page, and instructions for building the program on macOS. The source code, under the MIT licence, is at github.com/wujastyk/suci. Sūcī is written in Rust with the GTK 4 toolkit, and citations are formatted by the hayagriva engine using styles from the Citation Style Language project. Please post bugs and suggestions to Issues.
entry.summary: A fast BibTeX and BibLaTeX manager designed for humanities work on South Asia

entry.title: An Editing Screen for Saktumiva 2
entry.content:
This post is one of a series on the items in the Assets menu of this website, which I have written over the last two months together with Claude.

The problem

Our edition of the Nepalese version of the Suśrutasaṃhitā is made with Charles Li’s Saktumiva. Saktumiva takes the TEI transcriptions of the manuscripts, aligns them with the edition, and generates the critical apparatus. It has changed what a small team can do with a large text.

But the daily work of editing was still divided between three tools. The edition and its notes were written by hand in an XML editor. Saktumiva collated the files and produced the apparatus. The result was checked in a web browser. If, on reading the apparatus, one decided that manuscript K had the better reading, one went back to the XML editor, found the passage, changed the text, ran the collation again, and looked at the result again. Every decision meant a trip round all three.

At the end of October 2026 I wrote a short proposal for something better: a single screen on which the editor reads the critical text, the apparatus and the manuscripts side by side, makes decisions by direct action, and has every decision written back into the TEI files while Saktumiva rebuilds the apparatus in the background. The Saktumiva editor is the result.

What it does

The screen has three parts. On the left is the list of passages. In the centre is the text of the current passage as it stands in the edition, with the apparatus below it. On the right is each witness’s text of the same passage, with a button that opens the image of the manuscript page.

  • Words that have variants are underlined. Pointing at a reading in the apparatus and pressing use puts it into the text. The passage is collated again, and the former reading takes its place among the variants.
  • The text can be typed into directly. A reading that no witness has can be recorded as an emendation, with its note.
  • To add a note, one selects a word and writes. The anchor and the note are created together with matching identifiers, so the cross-reference errors described in the previous post cannot arise.
  • A mistake in a witness’s transcription can be corrected on the spot, in the witness’s own file.
  • When the automatic alignment of the witnesses has gone wrong, it can be corrected by hand, and the correction is kept through later collations.
  • Passages can be split and merged in the edition and in every witness file at once.
  • Publish writes the edition with a fresh apparatus, ready to go online.

Principles

A few decisions were made at the start and have proved their worth.

The TEI files are the only real data. The screen is a view of them, and nothing is kept only in the program. A file opened in another editor after a session shows exactly what was done.

Saving changes as little as possible. Only the elements that were edited are rewritten, and every other character of the file is left as it was.

Every save is a commit in git, so that each editorial decision is recorded and can be undone. Nothing goes online until the editor chooses to push it.

The collation is done by Saktumiva’s own code, running in the background on one passage at a time. A verse with five or six witnesses is a small problem, so the apparatus follows the editor’s changes almost at once.

Everything runs on the editor’s own computer. The only traffic to the outside is the browser fetching manuscript images from the libraries’ servers.

Using it

The program was written for the Suśrutasaṃhitā, but nothing in it is specific to that work. It will open any project that is laid out as folders of TEI files; my colleagues and I are also using it for other texts. There are ready-made programs for Linux, macOS and Windows on the releases page, and a tutorial for those who are new to Saktumiva, TEI or GitHub. Bug reports and suggestions to Issues, please.

The editor is under active development. It reached version 0.6.7 on 19 November, and members of the project are now using it for their daily editing. We are grateful to Charles Li, on whose work it entirely depends.
entry.summary: A local program that shows the edition, its apparatus and the witnesses side by side, and writes every editorial decision back into the TEI files

entry.title: TEI Scholar: A Plugin for Editing the Project’s XML Files

link.title: TEI Scholar: A Plugin for Editing the Project’s XML Files

entry.content:
This post is one of a series on the items in the Assets menu of this website, which I have written over the last two months together with Claude.

The problem

The Suśruta Project’s transcriptions and editions are TEI XML files. They are collated and published with Charles Li’s Saktumiva. In a Saktumiva edition, an editor’s note on a passage is not typed at the place where it applies. A small <anchor> element is put in the text, and the note itself goes into a <standOff> element at the end of the file, connected to the anchor by matching identifiers:

<anchor xml:id="SS.3.1.4-n1"/>
  ...
<standOff corresp="#SS.3.1.4" type="Note">
    <note xml:lang="en" target="#SS.3.1.4-n1">Text of the note.</note>
</standOff>

This is a sound design, but it is laborious to do by hand. The editor has to invent an identifier, type it twice without a slip, and scroll to the end of a long file and back, perhaps hundreds of times in a chapter. Mistakes are inevitable. When we recently checked the provisional edition files of the Suśrutasaṃhitā we found about 110 problems of this kind: anchors without notes, notes without anchors, and duplicated identifiers.

What the plugin does

TEI Scholar is an extension for the free editors VS Code and VSCodium. Its main purpose is to make a Saktumiva note behave like a footnote in a word processor. One presses a key at the point in the text where the note belongs, types the note in a pane at the bottom of the window, and saves it. The plugin creates the anchor and the note together, numbers them, and puts the note in the right place at the end of the file. Hovering over an anchor shows its note, and one can jump from an anchor to its note and back. Deleting the anchor deletes the note. Notes can be of different types, such as Note, Emendation and Testimonia, which Saktumiva displays separately.

It does several other things that we found we wanted:

  • Hovering over any TEI element shows what it means, which attributes it takes and where it may be used, with a link to the TEI Guidelines.
  • Files are validated as one types, against the TEI schema or the project’s own. The validation is done by Red Hat’s XML extension, using the same validator as oXygen.
  • It warns about duplicate identifiers and about pointers to identifiers that do not exist.
  • A menu switches between font settings suited to markup, to IAST, to Devanāgarī, and to Tibetan and South Indian scripts.
  • Selected text can be converted between IAST, Devanāgarī, Harvard-Kyoto and Velthuis.

Background

For many years most of us have used the oXygen XML Editor, which is excellent, but it is a commercial program and its licence is a real cost for students and for colleagues without institutional support. VS Code and VSCodium are free and run on every system. What they lacked was a knowledge of the conventions of our files. The first version of the plugin was written in October 2026.

The plugin is not specific to the Suśrutasaṃhitā. It should be useful to anybody editing TEI transcriptions of Sanskrit manuscripts, and especially to other users of Saktumiva. It can be downloaded from github.com/sushrutaproject/TEI-scholar-Codium-plugin, where there are instructions for installing it. Please post bugs or corrections to Issues.

For those who would prefer not to see the XML at all, the next post in this series describes a different approach.
entry.summary: A VS Code and VSCodium extension that handles Saktumiva footnotes, TEI help, and fonts for Indian scripts

entry.title: An Index to Singh and Chunekar’s Glossary of Vegetable Drugs in Bṛhattrayī

link.title: An Index to Singh and Chunekar’s Glossary of Vegetable Drugs in Bṛhattrayī

entry.content:
This post is one of a series on the items in the Assets menu of this website, which I have written over the last two months together with Claude.

The book

Thakur Balwant Singh and K. C. Chunekar’s Glossary of Vegetable Drugs in Bṛhattrayī (Varanasi: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1972) is one of the books that is always open on the desk of anyone translating Sanskrit medical literature. It lists every plant name in the Carakasaṃhitā, the Suśrutasaṃhitā and the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya in Nāgarī alphabetical order. For each name the authors give a discussion of the plant’s identity, often drawing on the commentators and on their own knowledge of the plants and of the drug markets, and then a list of every place in the three works where the name occurs.

Those lists of occurrences are extremely valuable, but in a printed book they can only be used in one direction, from the plant name to the passages. One cannot ask the book which plants are mentioned in a particular chapter, or which Sanskrit names the authors connect with a particular botanical species, without a great deal of page turning.

The index

The online index makes these questions easy. It contains:

  • 1,848 entries, with 2,187 headwords in Devanāgarī and IAST;
  • 30,342 citations of the three works, each one parsed into text, sthāna, chapter and verse;
  • 669 distinct botanical names.

One can search by headword, by botanical name or by passage. Typing a reference such as Suśruta, Sūtrasthāna 38, shows every plant that Singh and Chunekar cite from that chapter.

The book is still in copyright, so we have not reproduced its text. The repository holds index data only: headwords, page numbers, botanical names and citations. When an entry is opened, the search page shows that entry’s own part of the printed page, fetched directly from the scan at the Internet Archive by means of IIIF. The authors’ discussion is therefore read in the original, as it should be.

How it was made, and how far to trust it

All 568 pages of the scan were read by OCR. The headwords in the book are printed twice, once in Devanāgarī and once in spaced roman capitals, and this was a great help: the two readings were compared letter by letter, and each headword is marked according to whether they agree. About three quarters agree exactly, and about a tenth disagree and should be checked against the page image, which is always one click away.

The citation numbers come from OCR of small type. Errors are rare but they exist, so please look at the scan before quoting a reference. The botanical names are those of the book, in the nomenclature of 1972. Many formal botanical names have since changed under the supervision of the International Association for Plant Taxonomy. Wikipedia is a surprisingly excellent source of up-to-date plant names (e.g., Centella asiatica (L.) Urban).

The data and the programs are at github.com/sushrutaproject/glossaries, together with a fuller account of the method. The repository is laid out so that other reference works on Indian materia medica can be added in the same way. Corrections are very welcome.

For the scholarship, please cite the book itself. Corrections to Issues, please.
entry.summary: A searchable concordance of headwords, botanical names and citations, linked to page images at the Internet Archive

entry.title: Searching the SARIT and GRETIL Corpora

link.title: Searching the SARIT and GRETIL Corpora

entry.content:
This post is one of a series on the items in the Assets menu of this website, which I have written over the last two months together with Claude.

What it is

SARIT and GRETIL Corpus Search is a search page for two large collections of electronic texts in Sanskrit and other Indian languages.

One can search for a phrase, for all or any of a set of words, or with a regular expression. The search can be told to ignore diacritics, word division, and the difference between anusvāra and the class nasals, which matters a great deal when the same word may have been typed saṃkhyā in one text and saṅkhyā in another. The search term can be typed in IAST, Devanāgarī, Harvard-Kyoto, Velthuis, SLP1 or ITRANS, and the results shown in IAST or Devanāgarī.

Every hit comes with a scholarly reference to the text and the place in it, ready to be copied into a footnote. The results can be downloaded as a table.

Background

SARIT (“Search and Retrieval of Indic Texts”) is a library of Indian texts, mainly in Sanskrit, encoded according to the guidelines of the Text Encoding Initiative. I started it a long time ago, with technical help from Richard Mahoney. In 2013 Birgit Kellner and Sheldon Pollock joined, and the project grew considerably with support from the NEH/DFG Bilateral Digital Humanities Programme and the work of Patrick McAllister, Andrew Ollett, Jens Østergaard Petersen, Liudmila Olalde, Claudius Teodorescu, Dheepa Sundaram and others. The SARIT library includes several of the texts closest to our project, including the Carakasaṃhitā with Cakrapāṇidatta’s Āyurvedadīpikā, the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya and the Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha.

GRETIL, the Göttingen Register of Electronic Texts in Indian Languages, was started by Reinhold Grünendahl in 2001 and is much the larger of the two collections. Since 2016, Maximilian Mehner and colleagues produced TEI/XML versions of its texts, “Corpus TEI.” Support for GRETIL was withdrawn by Göttingen University after 2020 and it is now a static collection.

The texts of both collections have always been freely available. The difficulty has been the search. SARIT’s own search interface depended on a database server that somebody had to keep running, and such services are fragile once project funding has ended. For the Suśruta Project we need to be able to ask whether an unusual word or phrase in our manuscripts occurs anywhere else in Sanskrit literature, and we need the answer in a form that can be cited.

How it works

The new page has no server behind it. The texts are prepared for searching when the site is built, and the search itself is done in the reader’s browser. Because it is a static website it can be hosted free of charge and copied anywhere.

The page is built from my fork of the SARIT repository, github.com/wujastyk/SARIT-corpus, and from a copy of the GRETIL TEI files. The licence of each text is given in its own header and should be consulted before reuse. The About page of the site gives fuller credits for both collections. Bugs and corrections to Issues please.
entry.summary: A search page for the TEI texts of SARIT and GRETIL that runs in the browser and gives a citable reference for every hit

entry.title: A Searchable Bibliography and Indexes of Materia Medica

link.title: A Searchable Bibliography and Indexes of Materia Medica

entry.content:
This post is one of a series on the items in the Assets menu of this website, which I have written over the last two months together with Claude.

What it is

The site Dominik Wujastyk’s Bibliographies has two parts.

The first is a searchable index of my working bibliography for Sanskrit studies, Āyurveda and South Asian textual history. It has about 6,700 entries. One can search it in plain text or with regular expressions, filter by type of publication, language and year, and sort by author, year or title.

The second, under the tab Materia medica, searches the glossary databases of plants, animals and minerals that the Suśruta Project uses in its translations. At the time of writing there are about 750 plants, 220 animals and a handful of minerals. Each entry gives the Sanskrit name and the identification we have adopted, with references to the literature that supports it.

Background

I have kept my bibliography as a BibLaTeX file for many years, and it is the source of the citations in the project’s publications and on this website. Colleagues sometimes ask me for a reference, or for the file itself. The file has been in a public GitHub repository for a while, but a 4.6 megabyte plain-text file is not an inviting thing to consult. A search page seemed a better way of sharing it.

The materia medica files have a more particular history. When translating the Suśrutasaṃhitā we meet hundreds of names of plants, and the identification of each one is a small research problem. Early in the project we decided to record our decisions in one place, so that a plant would be identified in the same way wherever it occurred and so that the evidence for the identification would be kept with it. The files are written for the LaTeX glossaries-extra package, which prints the glossary at the end of our translations. Until now, the only way to read them was in those printed glossaries or in the raw files. The new page makes them available to anyone who wants to know what we think śleṣmātaka is, and why.

How it works

A short script converts the BibLaTeX files into data files whenever the repository is updated, and the search is done by the reader’s browser. There is no server or database, so the site costs nothing to run and should need little maintenance.

A word of caution. The citations are displayed in a simple author–date style that is generated automatically, and they have not been checked one by one. The bibliography is a working tool, with the gaps and inconsistencies that implies. Bugs and suggestions to Issues, please.
The underlying files are at github.com/wujastyk/bibliographies and are released into the public domain (CC0).
entry.summary: Dominik Wujastyk's working bibliography and the project's plant, animal and mineral glossaries, searchable online

entry.title: eTexts: Searching the Printed Editions of the Medical Classics

link.title: eTexts: Searching the Printed Editions of the Medical Classics

entry.content:
This is the first of a short series of posts describing the items in the Assets menu of this website. Over the last two months I have written a number of utilities and online services together with Claude, Anthropic’s AI system. Each was made to solve a problem that came up in the Suśruta Project’s daily work, and each seemed useful enough to share.

What it is

eTexts is a collection of digital reading editions of the classical Sanskrit medical treatises, each with its commentaries, in IAST transliteration:

  • Carakasaṃhitā, with Cakrapāṇidatta’s commentary
  • Suśrutasaṃhitā, with Ḍalhaṇa’s commentary (and Gayadāsa on the Nidānasthāna)
  • Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, with the commentaries of Aruṇadatta and Hemādri
  • Mādhavanidāna, with the Madhukośa and Ātaṅkadarpaṇa
  • Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā, with the commentaries of Āḍhamalla and Kāśīrāma
  • Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha, mūla only

These are the texts of the published editions, the printed books, what we call the vulgates (not Vulgate!), and not the result of our own critical editing. The About page of each text names the printed edition and the online source from which it was taken.

Why we wanted it

This tool arose directly out of the work of the Suśruta Project. When editing, translating and discussing the Nepalese version of the Suśrutasaṃhitā, we constantly need to look things up in the vulgate and in the other medical classics. Where else does this word occur? Does Caraka have a parallel to this passage? What did Ḍalhaṇa say about it, and did Cakrapāṇi say the same? The texts have been available online for years, most notably through the e-Saṃhitā pages of the National Institute of Indian Medical Heritage, but they are spread over several websites, each with its own interface, and some can only be searched in Devanāgarī or not searched across chapters at all. While the content of the NIIMH sites is excellent, the websites themselves have been quite unstable in the past.

What we wanted was a single, fast, stable search box for all of them.

How it works

The search page looks in the whole collection, in a single text, or in a single sthāna of a text. One can search the root text, the commentaries and the notes separately or together. Diacritics can be ignored, so that typing dosa finds doṣa, and regular expressions are available for those who like them. Clicking on a result opens the chapter with the matches highlighted. For the root text of the Suśrutasaṃhitā, each result also gives the page of the 1938 printed edition.

The search runs entirely in the reader’s browser. There is no server and no database. The first search downloads the index of the collection, and after that searching is immediate.

Each text can also be downloaded as a TEI XML file, either the root text alone or with its commentaries.

Background

The collection began in September 2026 as five separate websites, each built from pages gathered from an existing online edition. The TEI files were generated afterwards from those pages. In November we reversed the direction. The TEI file of each text is now the master copy, and the reading pages, the search index and the downloads are all generated from it automatically whenever the file changes. To correct a reading or improve the word division, one edits the TEI file and nothing else.

A useful consequence is that a new text can be added by putting a TEI file into a new folder of the repository. The converter was tested on all the texts of the SARIT library as well as on our own files.

The source is at github.com/sushrutaproject/eTexts. Corrections are welcome: please send them as Issues.
entry.summary: Reading editions of six Sanskrit medical works with their commentaries, in IAST, with one search across them all

entry.title: A Visit to Mahesh Raj Pant at the Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala, Kathmandu

link.title: A Visit to Mahesh Raj Pant at the Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala, Kathmandu

entry.content:
On 30 September 2026 we were invited by Prof. Diwakar Acharya to visit Mahesh Raj Pant at the Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala, the research institute founded by his father in Kathmandu. We were kindly received and deeply impressed by his wide knowledge of international scholarship and scholars. We were also impressed by his library, and by the work now under way to digitize his manuscript collection and publish the manuscript images on the internet.

The Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala

The Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala (संशोधन मण्डल), “The Revision Board,” is a private research institute for Nepalese history and Sanskrit studies. It was founded on 20 September 1952 by the polymath Naya Raj Pant (Nayarāja Panta) as a group of twenty-one scholars. Their first task was to correct the errors in Balchandra Sharma’s history of Nepal, published the year before. The institute’s work has remained true to its name: it corrects mistaken historical claims about Nepal by going back to inscriptions, documents and other primary sources. It also works on language, Nepalese culture and the Vedic tradition. Since 1964 it has published Pūrṇimā, a quarterly journal devoted mainly to history. After Naya Raj Pant’s death in 2002, his sons Dinesh Raj Pant and Mahesh Raj Pant took over the running of the institute. In 2011 it received the Jagadamba Shree Puraskar, one of Nepal’s highest literary awards (Wikipedia).

We thank Mahesh Raj Pant for his generous hospitality, and Prof. Diwakar Acharya for arranging the visit.

Web sources

  • Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala, Wikipedia
entry.summary: Meeting Mahesh Raj Pant, director of the Saṃśodhana Maṇḍala, and seeing his library and manuscript collection

entry.title: An Update to the Blog Post “Experiments with Claude” (17 July 2026)

link.title: An Update to the Blog Post “Experiments with Claude” (17 July 2026)

entry.content:
On 17 July 2026, Dominik Wujastyk posted Experiments with Claude on the Project’s blog, reporting the preliminary results of an experiment in using Claude to edit Suśrutasaṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna 6 (Ṛtucaryā). He asked Claude to study 23 chapters critically edited by the Suśruta team, alongside the witnesses on which they are based, to derive a set of rules or patterns capturing their editorial practices, and then to apply those rules to Saktumiva’s mechanical collation of chapter 1.6. The results were posted here.

Since then, Jason Birch has critically edited chapter 1.6 on ṛtucaryā without consulting Claude’s edition. He has recently compared his draft edition of the first 20 passages with Claude’s and offers the following general observations.

  1. Claude improved on Saktumiva’s mechanical collation of the witnesses by adopting K in more instances where the witnesses differ. In at least one instance, it correctly chose a reading of K that was the lectio difficilior and wrote a footnote explaining why the reading is plausible.

  2. Claude’s edition was limited by its inability to check the draft transcripts against the manuscripts. This might be possible in the future if Claude is given access to the manuscript images. Many of the defects in Claude’s edition resulted from mistakes in the draft transcripts; examples are given in the detailed comments below.

  3. Claude often uncritically favoured K (perhaps because it was told that K is the most important witness). As a result, it adopted incorrect readings of K. In quite a few instances, these incorrect readings were errors in the draft transcript, which Claude failed to identify. For example, it adopted triṃśatmuhūrttam (instead of triṃśanmuhūrttam), evauṣadhyau grīṣmaniḥsārā … bhavaty (instead of evauṣadhyo grīṣme … bhavanty) and śleṣmikāṇāṃ (instead of ślaiṣmikāṇān). Further instances are noted below.

  4. Claude included an additional passage in K that is not part of the original work and is marked as an insertion in the TEI code of the draft transcript. This passage does not fit the syntax of the sentence into which it was inserted. It is a clear example of Claude uncritically accepting the reading of K.

  5. Other problems include incorrect word division (e.g., dvimāsike naivaṃ instead of dvimāsikenaivaṃ), unnecessary footnotes, and incorrect punctuation of the edited text (although punctuation may not have been explicitly mentioned in the prompt).

The section “Significant differences” below gives concrete examples for each case.

Conclusion

It is clear that Claude has something to offer; its edition was better than Saktumiva’s mechanical collation. When it can do OCR of the manuscripts, it may improve further on its current edition. Nonetheless, its present effort resembles that of Housman’s donkey-editor, who, stuck between two bundles of hay, escapes the paralysis by uncritically choosing one bundle, arbitrarily called the “best,” which in this case was the oldest manuscript, K (Housman, 1937, p. xxxi).

References

  1. Housman, A. E. (1937). M. Manilii Astronomicon Liber Primus. Cambridge University Press.

Significant differences in 1.6.1–20

Significant differences between Claude’s and Birch’s editions of 1.6.1–20 are listed below.

1.6.3

Claude and Birch both adopt saṅkalayati and both write footnotes on this sentence, which is a nirukti of kāla. Claude’s footnote simply points out that K preserves the correct form saṅkalayati (as opposed to saṅkālayati in N and H). Birch considered this obvious and instead commented in his footnote on Ḍalhaṇa’s understanding of kāla.

1.6.5

Claude adopts triṃśatmuhūrttam, which is incorrect sandhi. K and N actually read triṃśanmuhūrttam, but the draft transcripts used by Claude had triṃśatmuhūrttam for these witnesses.

1.6.7

Claude did not insert an avagraha in āpyāyate ’rkaḥ. Claude and Birch both accept balavattarā, the reading of Kpc and H, which is the lectio difficilior, and Claude adds a footnote explaining why this reading is plausible. Further on, however, Claude adopts uttarottaraś ca, K’s reading in the draft transcript, which does not make sense. In fact, K, H and the vulgate read uttarottarañ ca.

1.6.9

Claude adopts varṣasaṃvatsaraḥ, the reading of Kpc in the draft transcript, which is unsatisfactory. Kpc actually reads varṣaḥ saṃvatsaraḥ, which is better.

1.6.10

Claude reads dvimāsike naivaṃ instead of dvimāsikenaivaṃ, an incorrect word division. Further on, Claude adopts sa vidāhāt, the reading of K, H and N, even though these witnesses have a plural verb. Birch adopts the vulgate reading vidāhāt, which is better.

1.6.11

Claude incorrectly includes the passage tatra … uttarāyaṇe, which was added to K and breaks the syntax of the original sentence. Claude states in a footnote that the passage was added by a later hand, an observation probably based on the transcriber’s TEI markup rather than on direct examination of the manuscript. Further on, Claude adopts evauṣadhyau grīṣmaniḥsārā … bhavaty, K’s reading in the draft transcript, but K and H in fact read evauṣadhyo grīṣme … bhavanty, the correct reading, which Birch adopts. Claude’s footnote points out the problem with the singular verb, but explains that it understands evauṣadhyau as a dual subject.

1.6.13

Claude adopts śleṣmikāṇāṃ, an incorrect transcription of K, which (like N and the vulgate) reads ślaiṣmikāṇān. Claude also adopts sañcayaprakopaśamā, a reading wrongly attributed to K in the draft transcript, and then writes a footnote stating that the correct reading, sañcayaprakopopaśamā, is found in H and N. In fact, K has the same reading as H and N.

1.6.14

Claude adopts haimanam, the reading of K, and then writes an unnecessary footnote noting that H and N read hemantam and hemanam respectively.

1.6.15

Claude adopts tūpayayujyamānāḥ, an incorrect reading of K, but then states in a footnote that this reading is incorrect. The error is in the draft transcript of K. Birch corrected the transcript and adopted tūpayujyamānāḥ, the reading of K, N and H.

1.6.16

Claude adopts tāsām, the correct reading of K, and writes an unnecessary footnote explaining why.

1.6.19

Claude adopts K’s uṣasyante (a transcription error for udhvaṃsyante). The better reading is H’s udhvasyante.
entry.summary: Jason Birch compares Claude’s machine-assisted edition of Sūtrasthāna 6 with his own critical edition

entry.title: A Vaidya’s Library in Kathmandu
entry.content:
Madhu Bajra Bajracharya is an ayurvedic doctor who was trained by his father, the late Mana Bajra Bajracharya (d. 2001). They descend from a famous lineage of Buddhist priests, as Mana recounts in his autobiography:

By caste, we are Shakya related to the Shakya of Kapilavastu, the birthplace of Lord Gautama Buddha. During the medieval period, following the principles of Bajrayana, the third advanced stage of Buddhism (following Hinayana and Mahayana), our ancestors received the consecration of Bajrayana. This consecration bestows the title of Bajracharya. To have this title, one must follow the principles of the “Heruka Chaka Samvara Tantra.” Those with the title of Bajracharya are the priests of the Newari Buddhists, one of the ancient inhabitants of Kathmandu Valley.

In 1937, I received my formal initiation as a Bajracharya, which I needed to be a member of the Bihara. In 1944, I received my consecration as Bajrayana, which I needed to be an authorized Bajracharya. In 1945, I married with Gyani Devi Bajracharya. Marriage is essential for Bajrayana practice. We have a son and four daughters.

— Mana Bajra Bajracharya, “Introduction”

Vaidya Mana Bajra Bajracharya’s Ayurvedic teachings were the subject of a book first published in 2009 (Bajra Bajracharya, 2009). In 2015, one of the book’s editors, Alan Tilloton, wrote to Dominik Wujastyk, about the Bajra Bajracharya library of books and manuscripts, noting that the collection was of important cultural value and its future was uncertain.

The collection

According to Madhu Bajra Bajracharya, his father learnt Sanskrit and collected manuscripts of medical works. He became known locally as a collector and was consequently offered manuscripts on many other subjects. As a result, the current collection includes not only medical works but a wide variety of material ranging from grammar and philosophy to narrative, devotional and astrological texts.

Many years ago, Madhu Bajra Bajracharya compiled a handlist of the collection, which he kindly sent to Dominik Wujastyk in private correspondence. This handlist indicates that the collection contains many hundreds of manuscripts, at least forty-four of which are on medicine.

I visited Madhu Bajra Bajracharya’s house, where he kindly showed me the collection. It is kept in three large metal cabinets, with each manuscript wrapped in cloth and tied with string. Unfortunately, the manuscripts are currently piled up and jumbled together, so it is impossible to find any particular item without unpacking the cabinets. A handwritten handlist was made in 2014.

A palm-leaf Carakasaṃhitā

Fortunately, during my visit Madhu Bajra Bajracharya managed to find a palm-leaf manuscript of the Carakasaṃhitā, which is recorded as the first entry in the vaidyaśāstra section of his handlist. It is incomplete and undated, but judging from the condition of the palm leaves and the style of writing, it looked very old to me, possibly earlier than the fifteenth century. This manuscript left me with the impression that the collection likely holds some very old and valuable material.

Texts and experience

I had the opportunity to talk to Madhu Bajra Bajracharya about the future of the collection. He feels that his children are not particularly interested in it, and he himself no longer needs it, now that he has fifty years of experience as an ayurvedic doctor. He told me that texts are useful for those learning Ayurveda because they provide general information, but that the most valuable knowledge comes from practising Ayurveda, through which one learns how to diagnose and treat people according to their peculiarities. Doctors, he said, need to treat people rather than illnesses; experience provides knowledge of both, whereas texts are limited to the latter. His father tried to address this issue by recording notes in diaries about specific cases. Madhu Bajra Bajracharya showed me these diaries, which are written in Nepāl Bhāṣā, and said they are the only books on Ayurveda that he now consults.

The future of the collection

Although the manuscript collection has little practical value for him, Madhu Bajra Bajracharya recognises its importance for preserving the history and heritage of Nepal, and he would like the collection to be properly housed and cared for after his passing. To this end we discussed digitisation initiatives, such as the British Library’s Endangered Archives Programme. Digitisation may help to safeguard the contents, but one would hope that the manuscripts themselves eventually end up in the care of a professional library that can preserve them for future generations.

The handlist does not mention a manuscript of the Suśrutasaṃhitā, but Madhu Bajra Bajracharya believes there is one in his collection. We therefore hope to return next year, with more time in hand, to unpack the cabinets and search the collection more thoroughly.

Web sources

  • Mana Bajra Bajracharya, Ayurveda in Nepal
  • Endangered Archives Programme, British Library
  • 2014 Handlist of manuscripts
entry.summary: Jason Birch visited the manuscript collection of the ayurvedic doctor Madhu Bajra Bajracharya
